title: The Vaccine Works
subtitle: Jonas Salk's polio vaccine, the Polio Pioneers' field trial and the Cutter Incident, United States and Canada, 1952–1955
intro: In 1952 the United States reported 57,879 cases of polio, the worst year it had known. Most of the paralysed were children, and every summer parents closed swimming pools and kept children home. That year, in Pittsburgh, Jonas Salk began injecting a killed-virus vaccine into children at two Pennsylvania institutions: the D. T. Watson Home, whose young residents had already been paralysed by polio, and the Polk State School, whose residents had intellectual disabilities and were wards of the state, consented for by officials. Those children left no words of their own that have been found; they appear here only in Salk's numbers.

Three years later, on 12 April 1955, Thomas Francis Jr. stood up in Ann Arbor and reported that the vaccine worked. Between those dates came the largest medical trial yet attempted: some 1.8 million 'Polio Pioneers', paid for by the dimes and door-to-door marches of the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis under Basil O'Connor. The first was a six-year-old in McLean, Virginia, on 26 April 1954. The trial was also a fight over method. Francis would evaluate it only if part of it used an injected placebo; the Foundation and most states preferred simply to watch unvaccinated classmates; Albert Sabin thought there should be no trial yet. The compromise ran both designs at once.

The record for this chapter is almost entirely official, institutional and press material, not diaries: published papers, foundation announcements, a university press release, presidential remarks, cabinet minutes, surveillance reports marked for official use only, and newspaper interviews. The form tags say so. Because all of it is twentieth-century material, entries are digests, quoting only US-government records and a few world-famous phrases.

The licences were signed the afternoon of the report. Two weeks later children vaccinated with lots from Cutter Laboratories in Berkeley began to fall ill, and by 7 May the Surgeon General, Leonard Scheele, had stopped the national programme. The Communicable Disease Center's new surveillance unit counted every case and showed a common source. Bernice Eddy, an NIH scientist, had found paralysed monkeys in her tests of Cutter lots months earlier, according to later accounts. Canada, using only Connaught vaccine, kept vaccinating.

Blame for Cutter is laid out here as positions. The government's own investigators pointed at Cutter's production and at testing standards that allowed live virus through. Critics in Congress blamed Oveta Culp Hobby's department and the haste of licensing. Sabin argued the killed vaccine was unsafe in principle, while Salk and O'Connor held that one maker's failure had been allowed to discredit a sound vaccine. A California jury in 1958 found Cutter liable without finding it negligent. By the end of 1955 the programme had resumed under tighter rules, and polio cases in the United States fell by half the next year.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Several key days are fixed only to the season (Salk's 1952 institutional tests, his family injections, Eddy's monkey tests, Sabin's June 1955 testimony) and are marked approx. Times of day matter on 12 April 1955 (morning report, 5:15 p.m. licences) and 7 May 1955 (4 a.m. halt).

eyes.name: Jonas Edward Salk
eyes.role: Virologist, aged 37–40; director of the Virus Research Laboratory, University of Pittsburgh
eyes.side: United States; University of Pittsburgh, funded by the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis
eyes.where: Pittsburgh laboratory; test sites in western Pennsylvania; Ann Arbor and Washington in April 1955

waypoints.label: D. T. Watson Home, Leetsdale, summer 1952

eyes.form: published papers, broadcasts and dated telegrams
eyes.authenticity: Salk kept laboratory records and published his results (JAMA, 28 March 1953); his radio address and later broadcast interviews survive as recordings. No personal diary for these years has been published. All of it is post-1928 material, so entries are digests only, apart from one world-famous phrase.
eyes.bio: Salk built a killed-virus vaccine from three types of poliovirus inactivated with formaldehyde. He tested it first on children and young adults in two Pennsylvania institutions, then on his own family, before the national trial. He was the public face of the vaccine, and many fellow virologists resented him for it; his own laboratory staff later felt he had not credited them.

sources.title: Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, polio history interactive
University of Pittsburgh, The Jonas Salk Legacy at Pitt

eyes.name: Thomas Francis Jr.
eyes.role: Epidemiologist and virologist, aged 53–55; chair of epidemiology, University of Michigan School of Public Health; director of the Poliomyelitis Vaccine Evaluation Center
eyes.side: University of Michigan; independent evaluator, funded by the National Foundation
eyes.form: dated letters and the official evaluation report
eyes.authenticity: His 1953–54 letters on whether to take the job are quoted in historians' accounts. His 'Evaluation of the 1954 Poliomyelitis Vaccine Trials: Summary Report' was released at Ann Arbor on 12 April 1955 and printed in the American Journal of Public Health (1955, vol. 45 supplement). Digests only.
eyes.bio: Francis had trained Salk in influenza vaccine work and was the man the National Foundation needed to make the trial credible. He agreed only if he ran the evaluation independently and if part of the trial used injected placebo controls, a condition that split the trial into two designs. His report decided the vaccine's fate in a single morning.

sources.title: University of Michigan School of Public Health, 1955 Polio Vaccine Trial Announcement
PubMed Central article on the design of the 1954 trial

eyes.name: Basil O'Connor
eyes.role: Lawyer, aged 60–63; president of the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis (the March of Dimes), Franklin Roosevelt's former law partner
eyes.side: National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis (private charity)
eyes.vantage_label: the patron who paid for it
eyes.authenticity: His announcements of 9 November 1953 and 15 February 1954 and his May 1955 telegram supporting Salk are reported in contemporary press and historians' accounts. No diary. Digests only.
eyes.bio: O'Connor ran the charity that Roosevelt had founded and that mothers' door-to-door marches and dimes kept funded. He backed Salk early, chose a fast field trial, and accepted Francis's terms to get it. He received a presidential citation for the Foundation beside Salk on 22 April 1955.

sources.title: PubMed Central article on the design of the 1954 trial
Eisenhower Library, Jonas Salk and Polio Vaccine (online documents)

eyes.name: Albert Bruce Sabin
eyes.role: Virologist, aged 46–49; University of Cincinnati and Children's Hospital Research Foundation; developing a live, oral vaccine
eyes.where: Cincinnati; Washington for hearings in June 1955
eyes.vantage_label: the rival who said it was too soon
eyes.authenticity: His objections are recorded in scientific meetings and in his testimony to a House subcommittee in June 1955 (reported in the press, e.g. Time, 4 July 1955). Digests only.
eyes.bio: Sabin believed only a live, weakened virus would give lasting immunity and thought a killed vaccine made from virulent strains unsafe to test on a million children. With John Enders he called the field trial premature. After the Cutter disaster he told Congress to stop production and inoculation until the vaccine could be made safe consistently.

sources.title: Account of the June 1955 House subcommittee hearing (reprint of a July 1955 press report)
PubMed Central article on the design of the 1954 trial

eyes.name: Oveta Culp Hobby
eyes.role: Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, aged 50; the first person to hold the post
eyes.vantage_label: the official who signed the licences
eyes.form: official remarks, cabinet papers and reports
eyes.authenticity: Her remarks of 22 April 1955, her cabinet paper of 29 April and her report of 13 July 1955 are in the Eisenhower Library (Hobby Papers; White House Central Files). US-government records: short quotation permitted.
eyes.bio: Hobby signed the licences for six manufacturers on the afternoon of the Francis report and became the face of the government's distribution problems. Democrats in Congress attacked her through May 1955. She announced her resignation on 13 July 1955, citing her husband's health.

sources.title: DocsTeach, Remarks by the Secretary of HEW on the Salk polio vaccine, 22 April 1955
Eisenhower Library, Jonas Salk and Polio Vaccine

eyes.name: Leonard Andrew Scheele
eyes.role: Surgeon General of the US Public Health Service, aged 47
eyes.side: United States government; Public Health Service
eyes.where: Washington and the National Institutes of Health, Bethesda
eyes.authenticity: His orders and press releases of April–May 1955 are recorded in PHS documents and the Eisenhower Library; the chronology is set out in Harper's Magazine (August 1955). US-government records: short quotation permitted, though none is used here.
eyes.bio: Scheele stood beside Hobby at the licensing, banned the Cutter vaccine within hours of the first reports, and on 7 May 1955 halted the national programme altogether. He then rebuilt it under new safety standards. His decisions made him a target from both sides: some said he had moved too fast, others too slowly.

sources.title: Harper's Magazine, August 1955 (archive copy)

eyes.name: Dwight David Eisenhower
eyes.role: President of the United States, aged 64
eyes.form: public remarks and press statements (Public Papers)
eyes.authenticity: His remarks of 22 April 1955 and statement of 31 May 1955 are printed in the Public Papers of the Presidents and held at the Eisenhower Library. US-government records: quotation of 12 words or fewer permitted.
eyes.bio: Eisenhower gave Salk and the National Foundation citations in the Rose Garden ten days after the Francis report and offered the vaccine's know-how to other nations. Within weeks he was defending his administration over shortages and the Cutter disaster, and on 31 May issued a statement meant to reassure parents.

sources.title: American Presidency Project, Citation Presented to Dr. Jonas E. Salk and Accompanying Remarks
DocsTeach, Statement by the President about the polio vaccine situation, 31 May 1955

eyes.name: Randall (Randy) Kerr
eyes.side: Polio Pioneers (trial volunteers), Fairfax County, Virginia
eyes.where: Franklin Sherman Elementary School, McLean, Virginia
eyes.vantage_label: the first child in the trial
eyes.authenticity: What he told reporters on 26 April 1954 survives only in press reports, summarised on a Polio Network page and in later local newspaper features. As a child in a blinded trial, it was not recorded publicly whether he got vaccine or placebo. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Kerr is the one trial child whose own words from the day were printed. He is named in contemporary and later published sources as the first of the Polio Pioneers. He stands for some 1.8 million children whose parents signed consent forms and whose names ended up on Francis's microfilm in Ann Arbor.

sources.title: Polio Network archive post, Polio Pioneer - Randy Kerr
Connection Newspapers, Polio Vaccine's Proud Pioneers (2004)

eyes.name: Bernice Elaine Eddy
eyes.role: Bacteriologist at the NIH Laboratory of Biologics Control, aged about 51
eyes.side: US Public Health Service, National Institutes of Health
eyes.vantage_label: the scientist who saw it coming
eyes.form: laboratory findings, known through later accounts
eyes.authenticity: Her safety tests are known from later accounts, including Paul Offit's book The Cutter Incident (2005); no contemporary diary or memo by her has been published. Dates of her tests are not fixed precisely.
eyes.bio: Eddy tested lots of the vaccine in monkeys for the federal laboratory and found that some Cutter lots paralysed them. She reported this to the laboratory's head, William Workman; her findings were not passed to the licensing committee, and she was moved off polio work. Her story is the strongest charge that the regulators had warning.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Bernice Eddy

eyes.name: Edward Roscoe Murrow
eyes.role: CBS broadcaster, aged 47; host of See It Now
eyes.where: CBS, New York (interview on the evening of the Francis report)
eyes.authenticity: The interview survives on film; Salk's answer about the patent is among the most quoted lines of the century. The exact broadcast date is usually given as 12 April 1955.
eyes.bio: Murrow asked Salk on air who owned the patent. Salk's reply turned a technical question about property into a moral claim and has been quoted ever since. Historians note that the Foundation's lawyers had looked into patenting and concluded it was not possible.

sources.title: Bunk History, Could You Patent the Sun? (Retro Report)

eyes.name: Neal Nathanson
eyes.role: Epidemiologist, aged 27; chief of the Poliomyelitis Surveillance Unit, Communicable Disease Center (under Alexander Langmuir)
eyes.side: US Public Health Service, Communicable Disease Center, Atlanta
eyes.authenticity: The numbered Poliomyelitis Surveillance Reports (marked 'For official use only') survive in CDC Stacks, signed by Nathanson. US-government records: short quotation permitted. With Langmuir he published the definitive analysis in the American Journal of Hygiene in 1963.
eyes.bio: The surveillance unit counted every polio case in a vaccinated child or contact and tested them against the lots used. Its reports showed the cases clustering around Cutter vaccine, a common-source outbreak. They gave the government the evidence to separate one maker's failure from the vaccine itself.

sources.title: CDC Stacks, Poliomyelitis Surveillance Report No. 8 (9 May 1955)
CDC Stacks, Special Report No. 2 (14 May 1955)

eyes.name: Paul Joseph James Martin
eyes.role: Canadian Minister of National Health and Welfare, aged 51
eyes.authenticity: His decision to keep Canada's programme going is documented in Canadian histories; his own account is in his later memoirs, A Very Public Life (1983–85). Digests only.
eyes.bio: Canada took part in the 1954 trial, and Connaught Laboratories in Toronto grew the virus fluid for it. When the United States stopped vaccinating on 7 May 1955, Martin kept Canada's programme running, against some resistance from Prime Minister Louis St-Laurent, because no case had been linked to the Connaught vaccine Canada used. His son had had polio in 1946.

sources.title: The Canadian Encyclopedia, Canada and the Development of the Polio Vaccine

entries.place: D. T. Watson Home for Crippled Children, Leetsdale, Pennsylvania
entries.headline: First injections given to paralysed children at the Watson Home
entries.digest: Salk's first human tests were at the D. T. Watson Home, a residential home for disabled children, on children and young adults who had already had polio. The Post-Gazette puts the pilot group at 43. Because they already carried antibodies, he could see whether his vaccine raised them without risking a first infection. No surviving firsthand account by any of the children has been found.
entries.source_note: Pittsburgh Post-Gazette polio interactive (43 children; 1952). Many accounts give 2 July 1952 for the first injection; not confirmed here.

entries.place: Polk State School, Venango County, Pennsylvania
entries.headline: Vaccine tested on wards of the state at Polk
entries.digest: At the same time Salk vaccinated residents of the Polk State School, a state institution for people with intellectual disabilities, including children who had never had polio. The children could not consent for themselves; as wards of the state, state officials gave consent for them. Historians note this was common practice at a time when few legal protections for human research subjects existed. No surviving firsthand account by any resident has been found.
entries.source_note: Post-Gazette interactive (summer 1952; 161 children and staff at Polk; state consent); Science History Institute, Distillations, 'Fighting Through the Fear'.

entries.place: Meeting of the National Foundation's Committee on Immunization (Hershey, Pennsylvania, in standard accounts)
entries.headline: Salk shows his antibody results to the Foundation's advisers
entries.digest: Salk reported to the National Foundation's advisers that his vaccine had raised antibodies in 161 children with no harm seen. The results turned the Foundation toward a mass trial within a year. Older virologists, Sabin among them, urged caution.
entries.source_note: PubMed Central article on the trial design (23 January 1953; 161 children). Meeting place from standard accounts, not re-checked.

entries.headline: On national radio, Salk says it works but asks for patience
entries.digest: Salk went on the CBS radio network to say that he had successfully tested a vaccine against poliomyelitis. He tried to damp the excitement, saying no vaccine would be ready for that summer's epidemic season. He became a celebrity overnight, which many fellow scientists held against him.
entries.source_note: History.com, This Day in History, 26 March 1953 (CBS national radio, evening).

entries.headline: The scientific paper appears in JAMA
entries.digest: Two days after the broadcast, the Journal of the American Medical Association published Salk's report on his human tests. The paper set out the Watson and Polk results in technical form. Salk appeared on the cover of Time the following day.
entries.source_note: History.com; Post-Gazette interactive (JAMA, 28 March 1953).

entries.place: The Salk family home, near Pittsburgh
entries.headline: Salk vaccinates himself, his wife and their sons
entries.digest: Salk injected himself, his wife Donna and their three young sons with his vaccine, boiling the needles on the kitchen stove. It was a statement of personal confidence as much as an experiment. Accounts differ on whether this came before or after the institutional tests; most place it in 1953.
entries.source_note: Science History Institute, Distillations (family injections, no date); History.com (himself and family before going public). Exact date not established.

entries.headline: O'Connor announces a trial without placebo
entries.digest: O'Connor announced the plan for a 1954 field trial: vaccinate second-graders and compare them with the unvaccinated first- and third-graders around them. There would be no injected placebo. The Foundation judged a placebo too much of a risk to ask of parents, teachers and health officials.
entries.source_note: PubMed Central article on the trial design (9 November 1953; observed-control plan).

entries.headline: Sabin and Enders call the field trial premature
entries.digest: Sabin, joined by John Enders, argued that the trial was coming too soon. They doubted that antibody levels in the blood meant lasting protection. They also doubted the safety of a vaccine made from virulent strains of poliovirus, such as the Mahoney strain Salk used for Type I.
entries.source_note: PubMed Central article on the trial design (Sabin and Enders thought the plans premature). Month not fixed.

entries.headline: Francis leans toward taking the job, on conditions
entries.digest: Francis wrote that he thought he would take on the evaluation, though he had not yet committed. His conditions were that the evaluation be independent of the Foundation and that the results be scientifically defensible. For him that meant a placebo control in at least part of the trial.
entries.source_note: PubMed Central article on the trial design (letter of 29 December 1953).

entries.place: Advisory meeting on the field trial
entries.headline: State health officers back placebo controls
entries.digest: At an advisory meeting, state health officers endorsed placebo controls. Francis had worked through them to press the point. The Foundation still held to the observed-control plan as late as 8 January, so the two designs now pulled in opposite directions.
entries.source_note: PubMed Central article on the trial design (8 and 11 January 1954).

entries.headline: Francis formally appointed director of the evaluation
entries.digest: Francis was formally appointed to direct the evaluation, after telling health officers in Atlanta at the end of January that he would accept. His Poliomyelitis Vaccine Evaluation Center at the University of Michigan would collect every record and announce the result itself. The Foundation would not see the numbers first.
entries.source_note: PubMed Central article (appointment about six days before the 15 February announcement).

entries.headline: A compromise: two trials in one
entries.digest: O'Connor announced a dual design. In some areas children would be randomly given vaccine or an identical-looking placebo, with neither families nor doctors knowing which. In others second-graders would be vaccinated and their classmates simply observed. Most state health departments preferred the observed design; Francis insisted on the placebo design.
entries.source_note: PubMed Central article (15 February 1954; 84 placebo areas in 11 states, 127 observed areas in 33 or 34 states).

entries.place: Franklin Sherman Elementary School, McLean, Virginia
entries.headline: Polio Pioneer No. 1 rolls up his sleeve
entries.digest: In the school cafeteria, Dr Richard Mulvaney gave six-year-old Randy Kerr the first injection of the national trial. Kerr told reporters he barely felt it, less than a penicillin shot. Some 100 children were inoculated there that morning, and a third-grader fainted in the line. Whether Kerr got vaccine or placebo was not announced.
entries.source_note: Polio Network post on Randy Kerr (9:35 a.m.; his words to reporters); Connection Newspapers 2004; NPR 2021 (first of some 100 children); Arlington Magazine (fainting child).

entries.headline: The evaluation centre starts receiving records
entries.digest: As the first injections began in Virginia, Francis's centre in Ann Arbor began receiving consent forms, vaccination records and lot numbers from the trial areas. Every later case of polio in a trial area would have to be reported, tested and matched to a code. The work would take nearly a year.
entries.source_note: University of Michigan SPH polio page (role of the Evaluation Center); day inferred from the trial's start.

entries.headline: The trial spreads south and west
entries.digest: Within days the trial spread across the country, paid for by the Foundation's dimes. A Mississippi newspaper reported an eight-year-old girl as the first child there to receive an injection, followed by about 170 classmates. Mothers ran the clinics' paperwork as volunteers.
entries.source_note: Saturday Evening Post (2025), citing the Jackson Advocate (1 May 1954).

entries.headline: Canada joins the trial; Connaught supplies the virus
entries.digest: Canada took part in the 1954 trial alongside the United States and Finland. Connaught Laboratories in Toronto supplied all 3,000 litres of the poliovirus fluid used to make the trial vaccine, grown by a method Leone Farrell devised. That made Canada a partner in the trial, not only a buyer.
entries.source_note: The Canadian Encyclopedia (trial in parts of Canada and Finland; 3,000 litres from Connaught). Martin's personal role in 1954 not established.

entries.headline: Injections finish; the long count begins
entries.digest: By early summer the three-dose series was complete. Some 623,972 children had been injected with vaccine or placebo, and more than a million others were observed. Through the polio season Francis's staff logged every reported case and had laboratories confirm the diagnosis.
entries.source_note: PubMed Central article (623,972 injected; over a million observed). Dates of completion not fixed.

entries.place: NIH Laboratory of Biologics Control, Bethesda
entries.headline: Monkeys injected with Cutter lots are paralysed
entries.digest: Testing vaccine lots from the manufacturers, Eddy injected monkeys with Cutter lots. Some of the animals were paralysed, which pointed to live virus left in the vaccine. She reported this to Workman, the head of the laboratory. According to later accounts, her findings were set aside and not passed to the licensing committee.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Bernice Eddy (drawing on Offit, The Cutter Incident, 2005). Dates and monkey counts not confirmed in a primary source.

entries.place: Rackham Auditorium, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor
entries.headline: The vaccine works
entries.digest: Francis presented his report to more than 500 scientists and physicians, with cameras and reporters packed in. In the placebo areas 33 vaccinated children were paralysed against 115 given placebo; in the observed areas 38 vaccinated against 330 unvaccinated. The vaccine was judged 80–90 per cent effective against paralytic polio. The university's press release opened with three words that became the headline across the country.
entries.quote: The vaccine works. It is safe, effective, and potent.
entries.source_note: University of Michigan SPH polio page (press release, case numbers); Francis et al., Summary Report, Am J Public Health 1955.

entries.headline: Salk speaks after Francis, and leaves out his team
entries.digest: Salk followed Francis to the podium and spoke about improving the vaccine and the dosing schedule. He thanked the Foundation and others, but not by name the members of his own Pittsburgh laboratory. Some of them, including Julius Youngner, later said they were hurt by the omission.
entries.source_note: Standard biographies (e.g. Oshinsky, Polio: An American Story, 2005). Not checked against a transcript.

entries.headline: The Foundation's gamble pays out
entries.digest: For O'Connor the day vindicated a gamble. His charity had paid grants totalling $7.5 million for the evaluation alone and had ordered vaccine before anyone knew whether it worked. He watched the announcement from Ann Arbor.
entries.source_note: University of Michigan SPH page ($7.5 million in grants). O'Connor's presence and advance purchase from standard accounts, not re-checked.

entries.headline: Licences signed within hours
entries.digest: Late that afternoon, with Surgeon General Scheele beside her, Hobby signed licences for six manufacturers to make and sell the vaccine. She called it a history-making day for the whole world. The advisory review behind the decision had taken only a few hours.
entries.source_note: Saturday Evening Post (2025), citing contemporary press (5:15 p.m.; six manufacturers); Harper's, August 1955 ('late that afternoon').

entries.headline: The Public Health Service clears the vaccine the same day
entries.digest: Scheele's Public Health Service, through its Laboratory of Biologics Control, recommended licensing on the day of the report. The speed answered huge public pressure to have vaccine ready for the summer. It later became the main charge against the government after Cutter.
entries.source_note: Harper's, August 1955; Saturday Evening Post (2025).

entries.headline: 'Could you patent the sun?'
entries.digest: Murrow asked Salk on See It Now who owned the patent on the vaccine. Salk replied that the people did, that there was no patent, and then laughed at the idea of patenting the sun. The answer made him a symbol of science given freely.
entries.source_note: Bunk History / Retro Report (1955 interview with Murrow). Broadcast date as commonly cited.

entries.headline: Canada licenses the vaccine too
entries.digest: Canada licensed the vaccine at the same time as the United States. Its programme would use only vaccine from Connaught Laboratories. That choice would decide how Canada weathered the next month.
entries.source_note: The Canadian Encyclopedia (licensed in US and Canada after 12 April). Martin's own action that day not documented here.

entries.headline: The President asks for a plan to share out scarce vaccine
entries.digest: Two days after the licences, Eisenhower asked Hobby for a study of vaccine supply and distribution. Demand far outran supply, and newspapers were already reporting black markets. The government had no plan for who should get the first doses.
entries.source_note: Saturday Evening Post (2025).

entries.place: Conference on the Salk vaccine, Washington
entries.headline: Hobby admits confusion over distribution
entries.digest: At a conference on the vaccine, Hobby spoke of the public's state of mind over who would get the vaccine and when. Her prepared remarks survive in the Eisenhower Library. Critics took them as a confession that the administration was unprepared.
entries.source_note: DocsTeach (Remarks, 22 April 1955; NAID 12166301); phrase as quoted in Saturday Evening Post (2025).

entries.headline: Citations for Salk and the Foundation
entries.digest: After Hobby introduced Salk, Eisenhower gave him a citation and said he could not adequately express the thanks of 164 million Americans and of people worldwide. He spoke of the parents and grandparents spared the yearly fear of epidemic. The citation praised Salk for offering seed virus and help to scientists abroad.
entries.quote: the countless thousands of American parents and grandparents
entries.source_note: American Presidency Project, Citation Presented to Dr. Jonas E. Salk and Accompanying Remarks (22 April 1955).

entries.headline: Salk at the White House, ten days after Ann Arbor
entries.digest: Salk received the President's citation in the Rose Garden. It credited him with sharing the method and seed virus with other countries rather than keeping them. The record of the ceremony does not include a reply by him.
entries.source_note: American Presidency Project; Eisenhower Library photographs 72-1322-1 to -4.

entries.headline: A citation for the March of Dimes
entries.digest: O'Connor received a separate presidential citation for the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis. Photographs show Eisenhower handing citations to Salk and O'Connor. For the charity, it was public recognition by the government of a trial the government had not paid for.
entries.source_note: Eisenhower Library, online documents (press release salk-c; photographs 72-1322-1 and -2).

entries.headline: Six children paralysed after Cutter vaccine
entries.digest: Overnight the Public Health Service learned of six cases of paralytic polio in children vaccinated with vaccine from Cutter Laboratories of Berkeley, California. Scheele banned the Cutter product and opened an investigation.
entries.source_note: Harper's, August 1955; CDC Special Report No. 2 (first phase began 27 April with 6 cases).

entries.headline: A surveillance unit begins counting vaccine cases
entries.digest: Use of Cutter vaccine was discontinued on 28 April. The new Poliomyelitis Surveillance Unit began collecting every report of polio after vaccination, with lot numbers and dates of onset. Its numbered daily reports went to officials marked for official use only.
entries.quote: Use of Cutter vaccine discontinued April 28.
entries.source_note: CDC Stacks, Poliomyelitis Surveillance Report No. 8 (9 May 1955): 'Use of Cutter vaccine discontinued April 28.' Founding date of the unit approximate.

entries.headline: Hobby to the Cabinet: quality before speed
entries.digest: Hobby presented a cabinet paper on the Salk vaccine and reported the Cutter cases. She told colleagues that production must never be speeded up at the cost of quality. The minutes survive in the Eisenhower Library.
entries.quote: must never speed up production at the expense of quality
entries.source_note: Eisenhower Library (Cabinet minutes and paper CI-24, 29 April 1955); quote as given in Saturday Evening Post (2025).

entries.headline: Eddy at the emergency meeting on Cutter
entries.digest: NIH director William Sebrell chaired a meeting on Cutter's manufacturing, and Eddy attended. It reached no conclusion about the cause, and the expert committee recommended continuing with other makers' vaccine. Her earlier monkey results had not reached the licensing committee.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Bernice Eddy (29 April meeting); Harper's, August 1955 (29–30 April committee).

entries.headline: Twenty-nine cases, twenty-six of them Cutter
entries.digest: Scheele's press release reported 29 new polio cases among vaccinated children, 26 of them linked to Cutter vaccine. The pattern pointed at one maker, not the vaccine as a whole. Vaccination with other makers' vaccine continued for another week.
entries.source_note: Saturday Evening Post (2025); Eisenhower Library press release on Cutter vaccine (salk-m, 30 April 1955).

entries.headline: The whole programme halted
entries.digest: After two days of meetings with scientists and manufacturers, Scheele ordered a complete halt to vaccination at 4 a.m. on a Saturday. That same day the unit in Atlanta recorded the first case in a parent of a Cutter-vaccinated child. Parents across the country were left with half-finished series.
entries.source_note: Harper's, August 1955 (4 a.m., 7 May); CDC Special Report No. 2 (first parent case, Tennessee, 7 May); Canadian Encyclopedia.

entries.headline: Canada keeps vaccinating
entries.digest: When the United States stopped vaccinating, Martin decided Canada would not. No case had been linked to Connaught vaccine, the only one Canada used, and his expert advisers backed going on. He held to this against some resistance from Prime Minister St-Laurent.
entries.source_note: The Canadian Encyclopedia; Martin's memoir A Very Public Life (not consulted here).

entries.headline: Report No. 8: 52 cases accepted, and one from Wyeth
entries.digest: As of midnight on 9 May the unit had accepted 52 cases of polio after vaccination. A new case in Pennsylvania, a seven-year-old boy, was the first linked to Wyeth vaccine, and a Maryland suspect was ruled not to be polio. The report, signed by Nathanson, set out predictions for further Cutter cases.
entries.source_note: CDC Stacks, Poliomyelitis Surveillance Report No. 8 (9 May 1955).

entries.headline: A common-source epidemic
entries.digest: Special Report No. 2 estimated the national extent of polio associated with Cutter vaccine: 59 cases in vaccinated children and 9 in their contacts were on record by 13 May. The timing and clustering, the report said, fitted a single source. It warned of more contact cases to come.
entries.quote: wholly consistent with the pattern of a common source epidemic
entries.source_note: CDC Stacks, Special Report No. 2, 14 May 1955.

entries.headline: Salk refuses more ad hoc meetings
entries.digest: Back in Pittsburgh, Salk wired Scheele that he would attend no more improvised conferences and asked for a committee with real authority. O'Connor sent a telegram backing him. Salk believed the vaccine was being blamed for one manufacturer's failure.
entries.source_note: Harper's, August 1955.

entries.headline: New safety standards; vaccination resumes
entries.digest: Two days after appointing a committee that included Salk, Scheele announced tighter safety standards for testing vaccine lots. Makers' vaccine was re-cleared in stages, and the programme moved forward again. The Public Health Service still would not say publicly whether it had found live virus in Cutter's vaccine.
entries.source_note: Harper's, August 1955 (25 and 27 May; PHS reticence in early June).

entries.headline: The President reassures parents
entries.digest: Eisenhower issued a statement on the polio vaccine situation, expressing confidence in the vaccine's safety under the new controls. It was an attempt to restore trust after three weeks of confusion and attacks on Hobby. Vaccination resumed within weeks under stronger quality controls.
entries.source_note: DocsTeach, Press Release, Statement by the President about the Polio Vaccine Situation (31 May 1955).

entries.place: House Subcommittee on Health and Science, Washington
entries.headline: Sabin tells Congress to stop the Salk vaccine
entries.digest: Before Representative Percy Priest's subcommittee, Sabin urged that production and inoculation stop until the vaccine could be made consistently safe. Enders and William Hammon took similar positions. A poll of the experts taken by John Paul favoured continuing, 8 to 3, with four abstentions, and Scheele reaffirmed his support.
entries.source_note: Press report of the hearing reprinted from the issue of 4 July 1955 (Time). Exact day not established.

entries.headline: Hobby resigns
entries.digest: Hobby announced her resignation, citing her husband's health, three months after she signed the licences. The same day she sent the President a supplemental report on vaccine distribution. Through May Senator Wayne Morse had called for her dismissal and Representative Emanuel Celler accused her of creating confusion.
entries.source_note: Saturday Evening Post (2025); Eisenhower Library (supplemental report, 13 July 1955).

claims.claim: Pilot group of 43 children and young adults already paralysed by polio injected at the D. T. Watson Home
57,879 polio cases and 3,145 deaths reported in the United States, the worst year on record
claims.evidence: National case reports as summarised by the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette; other sources round to about 58,000 cases and over 3,000 deaths

claims.claim: Vaccine raised antibodies in 161 children, with no harm observed
claims.evidence: Salk's report to the National Foundation's advisers, per PubMed Central article on the trial design

claims.claim: Dual design: 84 placebo-controlled test areas in 11 states; 127 observed-control areas in 33 (or 34) states
claims.evidence: Foundation announcement, per PubMed Central article

claims.claim: First injection of the national field trial given at 9:35 a.m.; about 100 children inoculated at the school that day
claims.evidence: 1954 press reports as summarised by the Polio Network; NPR 2021

claims.claim: 623,972 children injected with vaccine or placebo; over a million more observed; about 1.8 million Polio Pioneers in all
claims.evidence: PubMed Central article; University of Michigan SPH

claims.claim: Monkeys injected with some Cutter lots paralysed, pointing to live virus (reported as 3 of 6 lots)
claims.evidence: Later accounts (Wikipedia, drawing on Offit 2005); no primary record seen

claims.claim: Vaccine 80–90% effective against paralytic polio; placebo areas 33 paralytic cases in vaccinated vs 115 in placebo recipients
claims.evidence: Francis Summary Report and university press release (University of Michigan SPH)

claims.claim: Licences signed for six manufacturers on the day of the report
claims.evidence: Saturday Evening Post (2025) citing contemporary press; Harper's, August 1955

claims.claim: Six paralytic cases reported in children given Cutter vaccine; Cutter product banned
claims.evidence: Harper's, August 1955; CDC Special Report No. 2

claims.claim: 29 new polio cases among vaccinated children, 26 linked to Cutter vaccine
claims.evidence: Surgeon General's press release (Eisenhower Library salk-m), per Saturday Evening Post (2025)

claims.claim: National vaccination programme halted at 4 a.m. pending review
52 cases of polio after vaccination accepted by midnight; first Wyeth-associated case
59 Cutter-associated cases in vaccinated children and 9 in contacts on record by 13 May; pattern of a common-source epidemic
claims.evidence: CDC Poliomyelitis Surveillance Special Report No. 2

claims.claim: Canada continues vaccinating with Connaught vaccine; no cases linked to it
Cutter vaccine caused about 40,000 cases of abortive polio, 200 children with varying paralysis, and 10 deaths
claims.evidence: CDC, Historical Vaccine Safety Concerns: Cutter Incident (as cited by USC Scalar); Nathanson and Langmuir's 1963 analysis is the definitive study

convergences.label: The trial-design dispute is settled by compromise
convergences.note: Francis held out for placebo controls as the only defensible science; O'Connor and most health departments preferred observed controls as kinder and simpler; Salk disliked asking parents to accept placebo shots; Sabin thought there should be no trial yet at all. The dual design let each claim part of the result.

convergences.label: First Polio Pioneer injection, McLean, Virginia
convergences.note: For a six-year-old it was a shot that hurt less than penicillin; for Francis it was the first record in a year-long count; for O'Connor it was the moment the Foundation's money went into children's arms.

convergences.label: The Francis report, the licences and 'Could you patent the sun?'
convergences.note: In one day the vaccine went from verdict to licence to legend. Francis spoke in numbers, Salk in plans, Hobby in celebration; the licensing review took hours, which critics later blamed for Cutter. That evening Salk's answer to Murrow turned a product into a gift.

convergences.label: Rose Garden citations
convergences.note: The President thanked Salk for 164 million Americans and the Foundation got its own citation, while Hobby that same day spoke of public confusion over distribution. Five days later the first Cutter cases arrived.

convergences.label: The first Cutter cases
convergences.note: Scheele banned one product; Nathanson's unit began the count that would prove a common source; Hobby told the Cabinet quality must come first. Eddy's earlier monkey results became, in later accounts, the warning that had gone unheeded.

convergences.label: The United States halts; Canada does not
convergences.note: Scheele stopped everything at 4 a.m.; the same day the surveillance unit recorded the first case in a parent. Martin kept Canada's Connaught programme running. Salk believed the halt blamed his vaccine for one maker's failure.

convergences.label: New standards and the fight over blame
convergences.note: Salk and O'Connor forced a committee with authority; Scheele announced new standards; Eisenhower issued reassurance on 31 May; Hobby took the political blame and resigned in July. Each placed the fault differently: on Cutter's methods, on the testing standards, or on the haste of the licensing.

convergences.label: Congress hears the experts
convergences.note: Sabin told the House subcommittee to stop the vaccine until it could be made consistently safe; the majority of experts polled and Scheele said continue. The dispute between live and killed vaccine was now being argued in public.

ties.note: Salk trained under Francis at Michigan on influenza vaccine in the 1940s; the student's vaccine was judged by his old teacher.
O'Connor's Foundation funded Salk's work and the trial; in May 1955 O'Connor wired support for Salk's demand for an empowered committee.
Sabin championed a live oral vaccine and called the killed-vaccine trial premature; their rivalry ran for decades.
Francis took the evaluation only on condition of independence from the Foundation and a placebo arm, forcing O'Connor's dual design.
Scheele stood beside Hobby when she signed the licences on 12 April 1955 and carried out the halt on 7 May.
Eisenhower asked Hobby for the distribution study on 14 April; she reported to his Cabinet on 29 April and resigned on 13 July.
Eddy's laboratory was part of Scheele's Public Health Service; her warnings did not reach the licensing committee, the core of later charges against the regulators.
The surveillance unit's reports gave the Surgeon General the case counts behind the Cutter ban and the halt.
Murrow's question on See It Now drew Salk's answer about the sun.
Kerr's record, like every Polio Pioneer's, went to Francis's evaluation centre; the names later surfaced in microfilm Francis left at the University of Michigan.
When Scheele halted the American programme, Martin kept Canada's going with Connaught vaccine.
The President presented Salk's citation in the Rose Garden on 22 April 1955.
Sabin opposed holding the trial; Francis ran its evaluation and declared the vaccine effective.

threads_out.note: Thomas Francis and Jonas Salk learned vaccine-making on influenza, developing killed flu vaccines for the US Army in the 1940s in the wake of the 1918 pandemic; that work led directly to the formaldehyde-killed polio vaccine.

Boylston's 1721 inoculation figures and Francis's 1955 report both settled a fight over a preventive by counting outcomes among the treated and untreated; the Salk trial added a blinded placebo arm to answer the old objection that the groups were not alike.
Both chapters turn on children used by medicine without consent of their own: orphans who carried cowpox across the ocean in 1803, and wards of the state at Polk State School injected in 1952.
The Poliomyelitis Surveillance Unit traced Cutter cases to a common source by lot, date and place, the same logic of shoe-leather epidemiology Snow applied to a single water pump in 1854.
